sections.title: Sound of the letter I
paragraphs: The letter (I) /iː/ sounds like the short vowel in (Insel) /ˈɪnzl̩/, which means island. A vowel is a sound made with open air and no touch in the mouth. This letter has three different sounds in German speech.

sections.title: How to say it
paragraphs: For the first sound, lift your tongue high and push it forward. Keep your lips relaxed and spread slightly. For the next sound, push your tongue even higher and hold it longer. Spread your lips wide, like a sharp smile. For the last sound, raise the middle of your tongue close to the roof of your mouth. Touch your throat to feel your voice shake.

sections.title: Reading and spelling
paragraphs: In closed beats before several consonants, say the short sound /ɪ/ as in (bitte) /ˈbɪtə/. In open beats where you put strength, say the long sound /iː/ as in (Tiger) /ˈtiːɡɐ/ and (Igel) /ˈiːɡl̩/. When this letter stands right before another vowel, say the smooth consonant sound /j/ as in (Nation) /naˈtsi̯oːn/ and (Familie) /faˈmiːli̯ə/. A consonant is a sound made when the mouth blocks or narrows the air.

sections.title: Pitfalls to avoid
paragraphs: Do not turn the long vowel into a diphthong like the sound in bite or see. A diphthong is two vowel sounds in one beat, gliding together. Keep your tongue very steady until the sound ends. Also, do not swap the short vowel with the long vowel, because changing the length changes the word.
